accuracy.evidence: Every grapheme and example word was checked against the National Curriculum in England English Appendix 1 Year 1 table: igh (high, night, light, bright, right), air (fair, pair, hair, chair), ear (dear, hear, near, year), ear with the air sound (bear, pear, wear) and are (bare, care, share, scared). Phoneme counts were checked by segmenting: night n-igh-t 3, chair ch-air 2, high h-igh 2, fear f-ear 2, light l-igh-t 3. The lesson does not invent a rule for air versus are; it says to learn the common words in sets, which matches the Appendix's lack of a rule at Year 1.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented Year 1 phonics errors: sounding every letter (prediction 'do i, g and h each make a sound', challenge key 'each'), counting letters not sounds (count step feedback '5 is the number of letters', prediction chair 5 sounds, p3, m3, m9), mis-splitting graphemes (challenge 'cha' and 'hai' for chair), phonetically plausible spellings nite, brite, heer, chare (mend step, m1, m8) and over-generalising ear so bear rhymes with hear (ear sort step, p5, m4). The air/are homophone trap is handled honestly in the build step: squ + air 'sounds right, but we write square with are'.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagtgraph is built around a three-letter grapheme acting as one unit: a dashed slot in a picture word accepts only a three-letter chunk, the sound counter rejects the letter count, the spot step needs all three adjacent tiles before it underlines the team, and the sort is about the two phonemes of one trigraph (ear). flagdgraph handles two-letter consonants, flagvowel two-letter vowel teams and flagmagice the split digraph; none counts a three-letter unit. The lab_distinct gate passed under the 30% similarity limit against every other lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child discovers the idea by acting before the text confirms it: the moon picture plus n _ t only accepts igh, then the counter refuses 5 for night and accepts 3, the underline appears only once i, g and h are all tapped, and the ear sort refuses bear in the hear box with 'It rhymes with bear and chair'. Each completion line restates the rule just used, such as 'Count sounds, not letters: night is n, igh, t'.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions each have a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: 'Yes, 3 sounds' for i, g, h in night (disproved when only the whole igh chunk fits the slot), 'chair has 5 sounds' (disproved by the counter rejecting 5 and accepting 2), and 'ear always sounds like hear' (disproved when bear, pear and wear only go in the 'like bear' box).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Every wrong challenge choice has its own message keyed to the slip: 'letters' (counting 5 letters in light), 'split' (treating igh as 2 sounds), 'cha' and 'hai' (wrong split of chair), 'bear' (ear sound confused), 'nite' and 'nogh' (missing letters of igh), 'each' and 'g' (sounding letters separately), 'air' and 'ear' (picking a word without are). Six questions rotate so a retry gives a new item.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences of mostly one-syllable words and introduce one idea each (what a trigraph is, the four trigraphs, counting sounds, the two traps); the validator's family readability limit passed. Lab prompts are a few words (Word 1 of 5: how many sounds?) on big tiles. The adult text uses the precise terms phoneme, grapheme, digraph, trigraph, segmenting and blending.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches or warns, with no warm-up sentence; the content gate found no banned phrases and explanation overlap is under 12% against every lesson, including the digraph and split-digraph lessons. Every feedback line names the specific reason, for example 'hair is a word, but not this one. Hair grows on your head. We want hear.'

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark for all 6 steps: the picture and letter tiles are about 54 px, the four chunk tiles fit across 390 px, number keys are large squares, the hear/bear bins fill half the width each (labels enlarged after the first screenshot pass), and sentence tiles shrink to one line. A full-size button row under the canvas repeats every action as big tap targets.

accessibility.evidence: The walkthrough gate completed every task with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) reported no violations in light or dark. Every drag or tap has a button equivalent with a spoken label (e.g. 'Put igh after n', '3 sounds', 'ear sounds like bear'), and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with each feedback message so a screen reader hears the result.

sources: National Curriculum in England: English programmes of study, English Appendix 1 Spelling, Year 1 (graphemes igh, air, ear, are with example words)
Letters and Sounds (DfES 2007), Phase 3: trigraphs igh, ear, air, ure
